thread.title: Is The S&P 500 Becoming A Tech Index?

author: Power Hedge
title: Is The S&P 500 Becoming A Tech Index?
text:
Back in March, I published an article to Seeking Alpha that discussed how an outsized portion of the S&P 500's ( SPY ) total returns over the past few years have been due to a handful of technology stocks. These five stocks are Facebook ( FB ), Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Alphabet ( GOOG ). On occasion, Netflix ( NFLX ) will also be included in this group but until recently it was not large enough to have a significant impact on the broader index. Recently, this problem has been becoming worse and it has led me to pose the headline "Is the S&P 500 index becoming a technology index?"
It will not come as a surprise to anybody that the markets have been awash with liquidity for the past several years. Ever since the financial crisis in 2008, the Federal Reserve and other central banks around the world have flooded the markets with liquidity in an attempt to drive interest rates down and prop up the global economy. This has resulted in the markets being flooded with an excess of $18 trillion looking for a home. While the Federal Reserve has been trying to pull some of this excess liquidity out of the market as of late, it still has a long way to go and not all other global central banks have followed its lead. Thus, the markets are still faced with an overwhelming amount of liquidity.
One of the places that this excess liquidity has ended up is in technology funds, which have seen annualized net inflows of $37 billion this year. This is double last year's rate and more than ten times that of any other year in the last fifteen.
Source: Zero Hedge
These technology funds that are receiving such massive inflows are forced to find a home for it as funds oftentimes do not have the liberty to just sit around on mountains of cash even if the fund manager may otherwise think that valuations are too high to just purchase stocks regardless of fundamentals.
Thus, the technology funds have largely been using this money to purchase shares in the largest technology firms, the same ones listed above. As we would expect then, this has pushed the stock prices of these companies up. It also had the effect of pushing their market caps up and as the S&P 500 is a market cap-weighted index, it increased the proportional weighting of each of the companies in the index. As David Kostin from Goldman Sachs points out , the net result is that just four companies (Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Microsoft) were responsible for 84% of the index's upside this year.
Source: Zero Hedge
As we see here, when we add Facebook and Alphabet into the mix, we see that just six companies, all of them big technology firms, have been responsible for fully 99% of the S&P 500's total upside so far this year!
It is also interesting to note that these ten companies, eight of which are technology firms, were responsible for 122% of the S&P 500's upside so far this year. What this tells us is that were it not for these companies, the index would have been sharply negative in 2018. The fact that eight of these are large technology firms should not be lost on readers either since this has increased the already oversized technology weighting in the index and by extension S&P 500 indexed funds. Here are the current sector weightings of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ):
Source: State Street
As is immediately obvious, information technology accounts for an outsized portion of the index, accounting for almost as much as the massive healthcare and financials sectors (the second and third largest sectors respectively) combined! Perhaps even more telling though is the top ten single holdings of the ETF:
Source: State Street
As we can see, five of the companies that have been responsible for the index's performance this year are included in the top ten holdings. These five technology companies alone account for 15.16% of the index fund's total holdings. There is no other single sector with more than a single company in the top ten holdings of the fund, unless one considers Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.B ) to be a financial. When we consider that the S&P 500 is the index that is most often used as a proxy for the United States economy, this seems to be an awfully high concentration for just five companies in a single industry.
As a handful of technology stocks are now clearly responsible for the returns of the index and have grown so large that they make up an outsized portion of the overall index, the S&P 500 index funds are now beginning to look like technology funds. This seems highly unusual for the benchmark index for the entire United States economy. The last point here is critical. After all, a fund whose returns are dictated by the fortunes of technology stocks would not be so bad if that is what investors expected to be getting. However, the overwhelming majority of investors that are purchasing an S&P 500 index fund expect to get returns commensurate with the performance of the United States economy as a whole. That does not appear to be the case at this time, however.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
